This method selects a subset of representative training viewpoints from a large set of rendered images by clustering camera poses and filtering for image quality [S1].

The evidence explicitly describes a method that selects representative viewpoints by clustering camera poses (using 6D feature vectors of camera center and forward direction via k-means) and filtering for image quality (selecting the frame with the highest Laplacian variance, which indicates sharpness/image quality, within each cluster). This aligns perfectly with the claim.

Reassign images to blocks based on the expanded bounds [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that images are reassigned to blocks based on expanded bounds. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly describes a process where: 1) Images are initially clustered using KMeans on camera centers. 2) Axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) are computed for each block. 3) These bounding boxes are scaled up (expanded) using a scale factor vector s_AABB. 4) Images are then regrouped (reassigned) into blocks if their camera poses fall within these new, expanded bounds. This matches the claim exactly.

For each image $i$, compute the camera center $c_i$ and forward direction $z_i$ from the extrinsic parameters $R_i, t_i$ [S1].

The claim states that for each image $i$, the camera center $c_i$ and forward direction $z_i$ are computed from the extrinsic parameters $R_i, t_i$. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.3, stating: 'Given the rotation matrix Rn and translation vector tn, the camera center can be expressed as cn=−RnTtn, while the forward direction is derived from the third column of the rotation matrix, denoted as zn=RT[0,0,1]T.' The notation $n$ in the source corresponds to the index $i$ in the claim. Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.

Originating from methods for large-scale NeRF reconstruction and sparse-view Gaussian Splatting, this technique addresses the scalability and stability issues of training on all available views [S1][S2, unofficial]. [S1] introduces it for "Denoise-GS" to select representative viewpoints for fine-grained denoising. [S2, unofficial] introduces "Block Splitting" for "SCALAR-NeRF" to enable distributed training of local NeRF models.

The claim states that the technique originates from methods for large-scale NeRF reconstruction and sparse-view Gaussian Splatting, addressing scalability and stability. The evidence supports this by detailing two specific methods: [S1] describes 'Denoise-GS' (a Gaussian Splatting method) which selects representative viewpoints to mitigate instability and noise propagation (addressing stability). [S2] describes 'SCALAR-NeRF' which uses 'Block Splitting' to enable distributed training of local NeRF models (addressing scalability in large-scale NeRF reconstruction). The specific mechanisms described in the claim (Denoise-GS for representative viewpoints, Block Splitting for SCALAR-NeRF distributed training) are explicitly present in the provided source texts.
supported
